rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to ensure all 10 compounds elute within 42 min and reveal the overall elution window and critical pairs. The wide phi range and moderate slope maximize information while reducing the risk of a truncated run.

All peaks eluted well inside the broad scout, so now trim the gradient window to the actual elution window to improve time score while keeping separation high. Based on the scout, the first and last peaks correspond to roughly phi_e 0.11 and 0.54, so 0.20–0.50 is an efficient first compression test around the main cluster.

The 0.20–0.50 window was too narrow/weak and pushed the last compound into a long hold, so move to a stronger upper endpoint and shorter gradient to improve time while still focusing on the actual elution region. This should keep all compounds inside the gradient and test whether the critical mid-cluster pair benefits from a moderately steeper, better-centered program.

The current method has perfect resolution term, so the main opportunity is to cut run time further. Keeping the same phi window and temperature while shortening tG tests how much compression the closest mid-cluster pair can tolerate before resolution starts to fall.

At 8 min the run is fast but the critical pair (6,7) is under-resolved, while 12 min had full resolution with only modest extra time. A 10 min gradient interpolates between those results and is the most likely to recover enough resolution on the critical pair while keeping the time term near zero.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the goal now is to probe robustness and see whether a slightly higher starting organic can shorten the early empty space without sacrificing the critical 6/7 resolution. This keeps the successful slope and upper endpoint fixed while testing a small, targeted window shift.

The best methods suggest the useful elution window is a bit narrower than 0.15–0.65, with the last peak still comfortably inside the gradient. Lowering phi1 slightly should tighten the gradient window and can improve selectivity for the critical mid-cluster pair while likely preserving the zero time penalty.

Raising phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 improved the front end and preserved full CRF, so test one more small upward shift while keeping the successful slope and phi1. This checks whether the first peak can be moved farther from the dead-time region and the run compressed slightly without harming the critical 6/7 pair.

The best region is clearly around 0.15–0.65 at 10 min, and the critical pair is only marginally resolved there. A small increase in phi1 tests whether a slightly wider/stronger gradient window improves selectivity or spacing of that pair while likely keeping all peaks within the no-penalty time range.

The critical pair 6/7 is only marginally above the threshold and appears sensitive to selectivity, so a small temperature change is the most informative next lever after mapping the phi window. Lowering T modestly should increase retention and may improve that pair’s selectivity without risking loss of all 10 peaks or a time penalty.

Temperature clearly changes selectivity, and lowering to 35 C created a new critical coelution, so test the opposite direction. A modest increase to 45 C may preserve the good timing while improving or at least redistributing selectivity around the crowded mid-cluster.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and test a lower phi0 while keeping the successful 10 min, 0.65 endpoint. This probes whether widening the low-organic side improves the marginal mid-cluster separation enough to maintain a max score with a different robustness profile.

The maximum score at 0.10–0.65 and 0.15–0.65 suggests a narrow optimum; this run tests whether lowering phi1 while returning phi0 to 0.10 preserves acceptable timing and improves the marginal 6/7 spacing. It fills in the remaining key window combination around the current best conditions.

Both 0.10–0.65 and 0.15–0.65 at 10 min already achieve the maximum score, so the best use of another run is to test robustness of the stronger-start window against a slightly shallower slope. This will show whether the critical 6/7 pair gains useful margin at 0.15–0.65, potentially identifying the safer max-CRF method.

The max score sits on a narrow ridge near phi1 = 0.65, and we have tested adjacent windows except 0.10–0.70. This run checks whether widening the upper end while keeping the successful 0.10 start changes the crowded mid-cluster selectivity enough to reveal an equally strong but potentially more robust alternative.

We already have multiple max-CRF methods at 40 C, so use remaining budget to map whether a larger temperature shift creates a different selectivity regime. Testing 25 C is informative because 35 C and 45 C both hurt but in different ways, suggesting temperature strongly perturbs the crowded center and could reveal a reordered separation pattern.

25, 35, and 45 C all changed selectivity substantially, so 60 C is the last key temperature extreme to map around the otherwise optimal method. This final temperature probe can confirm whether 40 C is uniquely favorable or whether a higher-temperature selectivity regime gives a different fully resolved pattern.

With temperature extremes mapped and 40 C clearly optimal, use the remaining runs to define the edge of the max-CRF plateau in gradient slope for the second best window. Testing 0.15–0.65 at 8 min shows whether this equally scoring method has the same sharp loss of resolution seen for 0.10–0.65 when the gradient is made slightly steeper.

We have not yet tested the lower-left neighboring window to the best method. This run maps whether combining the lower phi0 with the narrower phi1 recovers the stronger 6/7 resolution seen at phi1 = 0.60 while keeping time acceptable, completing the local window exploration around the optimum.

This is the last untested local window around the 10 min, 40 C optimum family. It completes the neighborhood map and checks whether the faster front-end compression from higher phi0 can be balanced by the narrower upper endpoint without dropping the critical 6/7 pair below threshold.

The best 10 min methods improve slightly as phi0 rises from 0.10 to 0.15, but 0.20 begins to push the first peak close to the dead-time region. Testing 0.25–0.65 locates that upper boundary explicitly and checks whether the front-end compression still preserves full resolution across the crowded center.

We have shown phi1 = 0.60 is still fully resolved but carries a small time penalty, while phi1 = 0.65 gives the max score. Testing 0.55 defines the lower phi1 boundary more sharply and confirms how quickly the last compound moves into a hold when the upper endpoint is reduced further.

We already know 10 min is optimal on score, but a slightly longer run at the best window gives a final check of how much resolution margin can be gained for the critical 6/7 pair before time penalty becomes too large. This helps distinguish whether injection 5 or 6 is the more robust practical choice among the max-CRF methods.

With only two injections left and 40 C clearly best, this near-neighbor temperature test around the max-CRF 0.15–0.65 method checks whether the selectivity collapse seen at 35 C begins abruptly or gradually. It is the most informative remaining untested point near the optimum without repeating a method.

The optimum is clearly centered at 40 C, and the last remaining informative nearby temperature point for the best method is 50 C. This final run completes the temperature map around the max-CRF condition and confirms whether the selectivity loss above 40 C is gradual or already severe by mid-high temperature.
